notes.definition: Electromagnetic (EM) waves are transverse waves that transfer energy from a source to an absorber. They form a continuous spectrum, grouped by wavelength and frequency into radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, and all travel at the same speed (3 × 10⁸ m/s) through a vacuum or air.
explanation: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves. Unlike sound or water waves they do not need a medium, so they can travel through a vacuum such as space. They transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber. For example, the Sun (the source) emits infrared and visible light that travel through space and are absorbed by your skin (the absorber), warming it. A microwave oven (source) transfers energy to food (absorber); a radio transmitter transfers energy to a radio receiver.

EM waves form a continuous spectrum. This means there are no gaps: wavelengths change smoothly from very long to very short. For convenience the spectrum is divided into seven groups. In order of decreasing wavelength (and increasing frequency) they are: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. A useful way to remember this order is 'Rabbits Mate In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens'. Radio waves can have wavelengths of kilometres; gamma rays have wavelengths smaller than an atom.

All types of EM wave travel at exactly the same speed through a vacuum, 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300 000 000 m/s), and at almost the same speed through air. Because v = f λ and v is the same for all of them, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency and a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency. Higher-frequency EM waves transfer more energy, which is one reason why ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can be harmful.

Our eyes can only detect visible light, which is a very limited range of the whole spectrum. Within visible light, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest. Other parts of the spectrum have to be detected with instruments, such as radio receivers, infrared cameras, Geiger counters or photographic film.

Calculations with EM waves often use standard form. To find the frequency of a wave with wavelength 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, use f = v ÷ λ = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Use the ×10ˣ (EXP) button on your calculator and remember MHz means × 10⁶ Hz.
keyFacts: EM waves are transverse and transfer energy from a source to an absorber.
EM waves form a continuous spectrum.
Order (long to short wavelength): radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
Frequency increases from radio waves to gamma rays.
All EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum (and approximately in air).
EM waves do not need a medium: they can travel through a vacuum.
Our eyes only detect visible light, a limited part of the spectrum.
Red light has the longest wavelength of visible light; violet has the shortest.
Use v = f λ with v = 3 × 10⁸ m/s for EM wave calculations.

keyTerms.definition: A transverse wave that transfers energy from a source to an absorber and can travel through a vacuum.
The continuous range of EM waves, grouped by wavelength and frequency from radio waves to gamma rays.
A spectrum with no gaps; the wavelengths change smoothly from one end to the other.
The object that emits the waves, for example the Sun or a radio transmitter.
The object that absorbs the waves and gains energy, for example skin or a radio aerial.
The speed of all EM waves in a vacuum: 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think different EM waves travel at different speeds in a vacuum.
misconceptions.right: In fact all EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. They differ in wavelength and frequency.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think radio waves are sound waves because radios produce sound.
misconceptions.right: In fact radio waves are electromagnetic. The radio converts the signal they carry into sound with a loudspeaker.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the EM spectrum has gaps between the groups.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is continuous; the boundaries between groups are approximate and some groups overlap.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think EM waves need air to travel through.
misconceptions.right: In fact EM waves travel through a vacuum; this is how light and infrared from the Sun reach the Earth.

realWorld: Sunlight transfers energy across 150 million km of space to warm the Earth and power photosynthesis and solar cells.
Radio, television and mobile phone networks use EM waves to transfer information without wires.
Astronomers use telescopes for radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation to study objects in space that the eye cannot detect.
examTips: Learn the order of the spectrum with a mnemonic and be ready to write it in either direction (by wavelength or by frequency).
If a question asks which wave has the highest frequency, check whether the list is in order of wavelength; highest frequency means shortest wavelength.
Use 3 × 10⁸ m/s for all EM waves and enter standard form using the ×10ˣ button.
Convert MHz to Hz (× 10⁶) and kHz to Hz (× 10³) before using v = f λ.
When describing energy transfer by EM waves, name a source and an absorber.
summary: EM waves are transverse and transfer energy from source to absorber.
The spectrum is continuous: radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma.
Wavelength decreases and frequency increases along that order.
All EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.
v = f λ links speed, frequency and wavelength.

questions.question: What type of wave are all electromagnetic waves?
markScheme: 1 mark: Transverse
questions.explanation: All EM waves are transverse. They do not need a medium.

questions.question: Which type of electromagnetic wave has the longest wavelength?
markScheme: 1 mark: Radio waves
questions.explanation: Radio waves are at the long-wavelength end of the spectrum. Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength.

questions.question: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum can be detected by the human eye?
markScheme: 1 mark: Visible light
questions.explanation: Human eyes only detect visible light, a small part of the spectrum. We feel infrared as warmth, but our eyes do not see it.

questions.question: What is the speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3 × 10⁸ m/s
questions.explanation: All EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. 340 m/s is the speed of sound in air and 1500 m/s is the speed of sound in water.

questions.question: Which list of electromagnetic waves is in order of increasing frequency?
options: Gamma rays, X-rays, visible light, radio waves
Radio waves, visible light, infrared, ultraviolet
markScheme: 1 mark: Microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma rays
questions.explanation: Frequency increases from radio to gamma. Microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma is correct. The first list is in order of decreasing frequency, and the other two are out of order.

questions.question:
Light from the Sun reaches the Earth but sound from the Sun does not.
What is the reason for this?
options: EM waves can travel through a vacuum but sound needs a medium
Sound waves travel too slowly to reach the Earth
The Sun does not produce any sound
markScheme: 1 mark: EM waves can travel through a vacuum but sound needs a medium
questions.explanation: Space is almost a vacuum. EM waves need no medium, but sound is passed on by particles so cannot cross it.

questions.question:
A radio transmitter sends radio waves to a car radio.
Which statement is correct?
options: The car radio is the source and the transmitter is the absorber
Energy is transferred as sound from the transmitter
The transmitter is the source and the car radio aerial is the absorber
No energy is transferred, only information
markScheme: 1 mark: The transmitter is the source and the car radio aerial is the absorber
questions.explanation: EM waves transfer energy from the source (transmitter) to the absorber (aerial). They are radio waves, not sound waves, and they carry both energy and information.

questions.question:
Two electromagnetic waves, A and B, travel through a vacuum.
Wave A has twice the frequency of wave B.
Which statement is correct?
options: Wave A travels twice as fast as wave B
Wave A has twice the wavelength of wave B
Wave A travels half as fast as wave B
Wave A has half the wavelength of wave B
markScheme: 1 mark: Wave A has half the wavelength of wave B
questions.explanation: All EM waves have the same speed in a vacuum. From v = f λ, doubling f halves λ.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the electromagnetic spectrum?
options: Seven separate types of wave with gaps between them
A set of waves that travel at different speeds in a vacuum
A continuous range of wavelengths, divided into groups for convenience
A range of longitudinal waves of different frequencies
markScheme: 1 mark: A continuous range of wavelengths, divided into groups for convenience
questions.explanation: The spectrum is continuous; the seven groups have approximate, overlapping boundaries. All are transverse and travel at the same speed in a vacuum.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the frequency of a gamma ray and of a radio wave.
Explain why gamma rays have a much shorter wavelength than radio waves in a vacuum.
markScheme: 1 mark: all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum
1 mark: gamma rays have a much higher frequency, so from v = f λ their wavelength must be much shorter
questions.explanation: With v fixed, λ is inversely proportional to f.

questions.question: What is meant by saying that the electromagnetic spectrum is continuous?
markScheme: 1 mark: there are no gaps; the wavelength (frequency) varies smoothly across the spectrum
questions.explanation: The seven named groups merge into each other; there is no sudden jump in wavelength.

questions.question:
Describe the electromagnetic spectrum.
Your answer should include the order of the waves and how their wavelength, frequency and speed compare.
markScheme: Indicative content:
EM waves are transverse and transfer energy from source to absorber
the spectrum is continuous
order: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
wavelength decreases from radio to gamma
frequency increases from radio to gamma
all travel at the same speed (3 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum
eyes detect only visible light
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct order with clear statements about wavelength, frequency and speed.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): partial order or only one property described.
questions.explanation: A complete answer gives the order and links it to wavelength, frequency and constant speed.

questions.question:
A student makes this statement.
'Radio waves and gamma rays are completely different things. Radio waves are slow and harmless. Gamma rays are fast and dangerous.'
Evaluate the student's statement.
Use your knowledge of the electromagnetic spectrum.
markScheme: Indicative content:
both are electromagnetic waves: transverse, can travel through a vacuum, transfer energy
both are part of the same continuous spectrum
the student is wrong about speed: all EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum
they differ in wavelength and frequency: radio long wavelength / low frequency; gamma short wavelength / high frequency
v = f λ means same speed so higher frequency gives shorter wavelength
higher frequency EM waves transfer more energy, so gamma rays are more hazardous (ionising)
radio waves are generally harmless at normal intensities, so this part has some truth
conclusion: partly correct about danger, wrong about speed and about being completely different
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed evaluation identifying correct and incorrect parts with reasons, reaching a conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): identifies some correct and incorrect points with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about radio or gamma waves without evaluation.
questions.explanation: Evaluate means judging which parts are right and which are wrong, with reasons, then concluding.
